blocks.text: Quick verdict

NodeMaven is the better choice for multi-accounting and social media management: its IP Quality Filter and long sticky sessions reduce bans, unused traffic rolls over instead of expiring, and its $2.20/GB monthly rate undercuts SOAX's $3/GB Builder rate for US traffic. SOAX is the better choice for ad verification, app testing and large multi-country campaigns, where its much bigger network, carrier-level mobile coverage, ASN and ZIP targeting on Scale, and UDP and QUIC support matter.

NodeMaven and SOAX both put residential and mobile traffic on one balance, both offer city and ISP targeting, and both are popular with social media and ad-tech teams. SOAX brings scale (155M residential and 33M mobile IPs), UDP and QUIC support and country-tiered pricing, with credits that expire after 60 days. NodeMaven brings IP quality filtering, rollover traffic, cashback and a quality guarantee. This comparison weighs scale against quality for account and data work.

blocks.text: NodeMaven in 2026: what you get

NodeMaven is the quality-first option. Instead of handing out whatever IP the pool returns, it screens addresses in real time and lets you choose how strict the screening is. That matters most for account-based work such as social media management and multi-accounting, where a flagged IP can cost you an account. The price reflects it: $4.50/GB without a plan and $2.20/GB on monthly plans.

Strengths: IP Quality Filter screens IPs before you get them; Long sticky sessions for account work; Traffic rollover and cashback; Quality guarantee that pays for bad IPs. Weak spots: Smaller pool than mass-market networks; No datacenter proxies; Pay-as-you-go rate is double the plan rate.
SOAX in 2026: what you get

SOAX is a residential and mobile specialist known for granular filtering. Its 2026 pricing replaced fixed GB bundles with plans (Sandbox, Builder, Team, Scale, Enterprise) that include credits, and the credit burn rate depends on the exit country's tier. That makes SOAX cheap for some geographies and expensive for low-volume US work. The network is large (155M residential, 33M mobile advertised) and supports protocols few competitors offer, including UDP and QUIC.

Strengths: Residential and mobile on one balance; UDP and QUIC support alongside SOCKS5; Large pool with city and ISP targeting on every plan; Cheap traffic for Tier 2 and Tier 3 countries. Weak spots: Credits expire after 60 days; US traffic is expensive on small plans; Datacenter and ISP proxies were discontinued.
Pricing: NodeMaven vs SOAX

NodeMaven charges $4.50/GB pay-as-you-go and $2.20/GB on monthly plans, with residential and mobile traffic on one balance. A $3.50 trial includes 750 MB. Unused traffic rolls over, and you earn up to 10% cashback on used traffic. ISP proxies start at $2.99 per IP with unlimited traffic.

SOAX bills prepaid credits. For US (Tier 1) traffic, the no-fee Sandbox plan costs $5/GB, Builder ($200/month) $3/GB, Team ($500/month) $2.20/GB, and Scale ($1,500/month) $1.50/GB; cheaper countries cost less (Tier 3 from $2/GB on Sandbox). Credits expire 60 days after purchase, and SOAX counts traffic in both directions.

Buying 10 GB, you would pay about $45 with NodeMaven and $50 with SOAX: a 10% saving in NodeMaven's favour. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $220 with NodeMaven and $300 with SOAX: a 27% saving in NodeMaven's favour. The sticker price is only half of it. NodeMaven's unused traffic carries forward, while SOAX's does not (credits expire 60 days after they are added), so if your usage swings from month to month NodeMaven can work out cheaper than the per-GB numbers suggest.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

By advertised size, SOAX (155M residential + 33M mobile) is about 5.2x larger than NodeMaven (30M+ residential + 250K mobile). Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, NodeMaven lists 150+ countries and SOAX lists 195. On targeting, NodeMaven offers country, region, city and ISP, while SOAX offers country, region, city and ISP; ASN and ZIP on Scale plans.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, NodeMaven offers rotating or long sticky sessions (multi-day), and SOAX offers rotating or sticky; mobile sessions up to 60 minutes. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?
General web scraping: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: a large pool and its own error headers help debugging. How NodeMaven compares: the quality filter matters less for high-rotation crawling.

SERP and rank tracking: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: city and ISP targeting for local results. The limitation on the NodeMaven side: workable, but you pay a premium for filtering you may not need.

Social media and multi-account management: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With NodeMaven: pre-screened, low-fraud-score IPs with long sticky sessions. With SOAX: mobile IPs on the same balance as residential. Run the same small test on both before committing.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: granular location filters. How NodeMaven compares: fine for light checks.
Ad verification and geo-testing: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: ISP, ASN and carrier-level targeting. How NodeMaven compares: good quality but a smaller pool.

Tight budgets: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. NodeMaven: mid-priced on plans, expensive on PAYG. SOAX: cheap in Tier 3 countries but pricey for small US jobs. Let price and the countries you need decide.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. NodeMaven: $3.50 trial with 750 MB. SOAX: Paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99. Verification and payment rules differ too. NodeMaven: Standard. SOAX: Verification for postpaid and enterprise terms. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test NodeMaven and SOAX before you commit
The quickest way to choose between NodeMaven and SOAX is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (NodeMaven: $3.50 trial with 750 MB; SOAX: paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, NodeMaven comes out ahead in 0, SOAX in 4, and 2 are ties. That makes SOAX the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: NodeMaven is strongest for social media and multi-account management, while SOAX is strongest for mobile-first work such as app testing and social platforms. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
